tagline: Six miles under the leaves, through the Great Swamp.
intro: Route 110 leaves Route 138 at West Kingston and runs six miles south to US 1, a narrow road with narrow shoulders. In long stretches the trees on either side meet overhead, and mountain laurel and rhododendron grow right to the pavement. The road bends over glacial hills and kettle holes, past stone walls from old farms, and each curve hides what comes next.

Neighbors once organized against state plans to widen it, and the state settled for repaving. In 1994 Scenic America counted it among the ten most endangered scenic roads in the country, and the 1999 stewardship plan asked that the road not be promoted for tourism.
season: Spring, when the roadside rhododendron and mountain laurel are in bloom.

moments.title: Larkin Pond
moments.text: Near the northern end the road runs right beside an undeveloped pond, and with woods closed in north and south of it, the long view across the water comes as a surprise.

moments.title: Great Swamp
moments.text: South of the pond the road rides raised, flat and straight for about a mile and a quarter, looking over the roadside growth into the middle height of the swamp's canopy.

moments.title: Tuckertown Four Corners
moments.text: On high ground south of the swamp sits a small village, which the 1999 plan described as a town recreation park, a Grange and several homes.

sources.label: RIDOT, Ministerial Road Stewardship Plan (1999), pages 1 to 7
